headline: Public staff should know the 2027 campaign rules before March
dek: About 260,000 people work for the state or its enterprises. The Election Commission has promised guidance, but not yet a date for a draft or a word on what it will say.
paragraphs: Of the roughly 690,000 formal jobs in the Irad Special Economic Zone, about 260,000, some 38 per cent, are in the public sector and state enterprises. They include teachers, clinic staff and the clerks of city and district offices. This week Mejlis deputy Kseniya Shubina asked the Territorial Election Commission whether such staff may campaign for a ticket, may be asked to speak for one at work, and what protects them if they say no. The question would be as fair from any deputy, and as useful to any ticket, so it deserves a plain answer.

So far the answer is a promise. Chairman Daniyar Borubaev says the preliminary calendar, Decision 2026/4, fixes dates and does not deal with staff conduct, and that the Commission's guidance will appear "before nominations open on 1 June". He did not say what the guidance will contain, or whether staff conduct is in it. Register revision starts on 1 March. By the Commission's own timetable, the people with most at stake would see the rules after the work of the election has begun.

That is the weakness. Dr Aruuke Jakypova of the TSU Institute of Sociology points out that staff who will be asked to man polling stations, collect signatures or attend meetings plan their autumn well before June, and that a rule arriving after nominations open reaches them once habits are set. Ms Shubina puts it simply: a teacher should know on 1 September what she may be asked on 1 October. The Teachers' and Educators' Union, whose chair says it does not choose candidates, wants to know "where the line is, and who they can ask". A Chu District clerk wants it in writing, so that he and his supervisor are reading the same page.

The Herald has heard no account of anyone being pressed, and it does not suggest otherwise. That is the point. Rules are cheapest to write before there is a dispute to settle, and they protect the supervisor who does not want to be accused of pressure as much as the clerk who does not want to give it.

The Ministries of Education and Health, which employ most of those concerned, offered no comment, and the Commission has not said whether it will consult them or the unions. We ask for three things. First, that the Commission publish a draft of its guidance, with a section on staff conduct, by 1 March, and take written comments. Second, that the final text say in plain words what a public employee may be asked to do, what may not be demanded, and which office will answer a question or a complaint. Third, that each ministry and city and district administration undertake to give the text to its staff in writing, in the languages they read.

None of this decides who wins in November 2027. It decides whether, afterwards, 260,000 people and their neighbours can say they knew the rules. The Commission has the calendar and the authority. It should now name a date for the draft.
